To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) ConvNets can be trained to extract information from FIM images that is predictive of process stress states, and 2) a "data pooling strategy" can be used to reduce the number of images required to train a ConvNet classifier.

deep ConvNet-based classifiers can be trained to predict the process or stress conditions that produced protein subvisible particles with near perfect accuracy using as few as twenty particles imaged by FIM.

we developed a new method to classify subvisible protein particles in flow imaging microscopy data using a deep convolutional neural network, and that this method can be applied to a variety of different particle types in different formulations, and can differentiate between particles from different process conditions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and validation of a deep learning-based approach to particle characterization using flow imaging microscopy.
applying state-of-the-art machine learning techniques to the analysis of FIM data to improve the efficiency and accuracy of protein particle characterization.
the use of deep learning methods to extract information from images of subvisible particles in protein formulations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

our ConvNets-based classifier is able to extract information from FIM images that is predictive of particle formation conditions, and that this approach may be a useful tool for protein formulation process monitoring.
the proposed method is a novel approach to particle classification that is capable of analyzing raw FIM data and extracting useful information from it.
the ConvNets are capable of extracting information from FIM images that is not readily apparent in the low-dimensional lists of morphological features commonly used in the pharmaceutical industry.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that ConvNets can be used to extract information from FIM images of subvisible particles to differentiate protein formulations with high fidelity, and that this approach can be used to analyze FIM images of proteins with different molecular weights and different particle types.
the use of ConvNets in combination with a data pooling strategy can be used to develop a robust and predictive classifier for protein particles in FIM images.
we demonstrate a new supervised learning technique that leverages ConvNets to classify raw images in order for the prediction of the process conditions that produced the particles in the images.
The main takeaway from our work is that

ConvNets can be applied to raw FIM images of subvisible particles in order to extract predictive information that can be used to identify the conditions that produce a variety of different types of particles.
ConvNets, in combination with the appropriate data pooling strategy, can be used to extract predictive information encoded in raw FIM images without requiring the use of any morphological features.
ConvNets can be applied to FIM data to extract information about the underlying physical properties of particles that is not readily apparent to humans.
